           BEFORE THE CORPORATION COMMISSION OF THE STATE OF OKLAHOMA

                                                Kimber L. Shoop
                                               Rebuttal Testimony

    1    Q.    Please state your name and business address.
    2    A.    My name is Kimber L. Shoop. My business address is 321 North Harvey, Oklahoma City,
    3          Oklahoma 73102.
    4
    5    Q.    Are you the same Kimber L. Shoop who filed Direct Testimony in this case on June
    6          17, 2026?
    7    A.    Yes, I am.
    8
    9                                   PURPOSE AND OVERVIEW
   10    Q.    What is the purpose of your Rebuttal Testimony?
   11    A.    In their Responsive Testimonies, intervenors generally accept the need for a separate large-
   12          load framework. My Rebuttal Testimony responds to intervenor recommendations and
   13          criticisms concerning the Extra Large Power and Light (“XLPL”) tariff’s applicability and
   14          customer classifications; proposals for Commission review of individual agreements and
   15          related resource-adequacy and load-ramp protections; proposals that would permit XLPL
   16          customers to obtain generation outside OG&E’s bundled service framework, referred to
   17          here as “Delivery Only Deregulated Generation Election” or “DODGE” proposals; and the
   18          requested regulatory asset for portfolio optimization software. Importantly, I also explain
   19          why the Commission should preserve OG&E’s integrated regulatory framework and the
   20          XLPL tariff’s application to comparable extra-large service obligations.
   21
   22    Q.    Does OG&E agree that existing customers must be protected?
   23    A.    Yes.   That objective is central to the filing.      The tariff requires customer-funded
   24          transmission and distribution infrastructure through Contributions in Aid of Construction
   25          (“CIAC”), long-term commitments, minimum billing obligations, collateral, early
   26          termination and capacity-reduction fees, and ongoing Commission review of potential
   27          adverse rate impacts. The Customer Class Protection Charge provides an additional
   28          mechanism if a future cost-of-service analysis demonstrates an adverse impact. OG&E
         Rebuttal Testimony of Kimber L. Shoop                                                Page 2 of 34
         Case No. PUD2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 64 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/05/2026 - PAGE 3 OF 41




    1          believes that the various DODGE proposals not only have legal infirmities but are ill-
    2          advised on a policy basis because they would degrade the non-XLPL customer benefits of
    3          adding these XLPL customers to the grid and add only downside risk to other customers.
    4
    5    Q.    Who are OG&E’s other rebuttal witnesses, and what subjects do they address?
    6    A.    OG&E presents rebuttal testimony from five additional witnesses. Gwin Cash addresses
    7          incremental-load applicability and metering, minimum billing demand and energy, the
    8          Customer Class Protection Charge and customer-impact methodology, allocation factors,
    9          the Customer Affordability Charge and Reservation Charge, and class rate design and
   10          billing determinants.
   11                  John Laws addresses customer protections involving CIAC, collateral, contract
   12          term and renewal, termination and capacity-reduction fees, Preliminary Agreements, late-
   13          payment provisions, and CIAC review, refund, and self-build proposals.
   14                  Kelly Riley addresses interruptible service for XLPL customers and resource
   15          planning issues related to DODGE proposals.
   16                  Adam    Snapp    addresses   the   proposed    power-factor    requirement    and
   17          recommendations concerning Grid Enhancing Technologies and other transmission
   18          alternatives.
   19                  Matthew DeCourcey also addressees some rebuttal topics, including tariff surveys
   20          and peer comparisons on which several intervenors rely, the tariff’s applicability, the
   21          minimum term, termination and capacity reduction fees, collateral and billing minimum
   22          requirements, the class rate design determinants and the Customer Class Protection Charge,
   23          the rate benefit analysis, and the various DODGE proposals.
   24
   25                                         APPLICABILITY
   26   Q.     Why did OG&E propose a tariff applicable to more than one type of extra-large
   27          customer, regardless of industry classification?
   28    A.    The relevant system and financial risks are created by the size and nature of the electric
   29          service obligation, not solely by the customer’s industry type. A new or changed service
   30          obligation of 75 MW or more can require significant planning, capacity, transmission, and

         Rebuttal Testimony of Kimber L. Shoop                                              Page 3 of 34
         Case No. PUD2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 64 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/05/2026 - PAGE 4 OF 41




    1          operational commitments. OG&E designed the three customer types to ensure that
    2          comparable large service obligations receive comparable protections.
    3                 When OG&E must plan for, procure capacity for, and construct infrastructure to
    4          serve a 75 MW or larger obligation, the exposure to other classes is identical regardless of
    5          industry. The generation is the same, the transmission is the same, and the stranded-cost
    6          risk on departure is the same. A rule applying these protections to a 200 MW data center
    7          but withholding them from a 200 MW industrial facility imposing the identical obligation
    8          would not serve the customers HB 2992 was enacted to protect—it would expose them.
    9
   10    Q.    Walmart witness Marchand and Oklahoma Industrial Energy Consumers (“OIEC”)
   11          witness Dauphinais both recommend changes to the tariff’s definitions. What do they
   12          propose?
   13    A.    Both recommend an exclusion for residential, commercial, agricultural, and industrial
   14          ratepayers. Mr. Marchand directs that recommendation at the XLPL definition of Large
   15          Load Customer and the T&CXLLC definition of Customer; 1 Mr. Dauphinais at the
   16          T&CXLLC definition of Customer. 2
   17
   18    Q.    Does OG&E dispute what the statutory definition says?
   19    A.    No. OG&E reads HB 2992 the same way these witnesses do. The disagreement is over
   20          what follows from it.
   21                 HB 2992 directs that all electric suppliers shall establish separate terms and
   22          conditions and separate tariffs applicable to large load customers, and sets the minimum
   23          standards those instruments must contain. It is a mandate identifying the customers for
   24          whom a separate tariff is required—not a limit on the Commission’s authority to apply
   25          comparable terms where comparable obligations arise. In fact, HB 2992 specifically states
   26          that “the Oklahoma Corporation Commission shall have exclusive jurisdiction to enforce
   27          the provisions of this act within its authority.” 17 Okla. Stat. §905 (2026). It is certainly
   28          within the Commission’s authority to go beyond the minimum types of large load

         2
               Dauphinais Responsive, 8:34–37.
         Rebuttal Testimony of Kimber L. Shoop                                                 Page 4 of 34
         Case No. PUD2026-000046
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 64 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/05/2026 - PAGE 5 OF 41




    1          customers and ensure that other customers are protected from all large loads that create an
    2          obligation to serve in excess of 75 MW. No intervenor witness identifies any statute or
    3          legal argument preventing the Commission from exercising its authority to include
    4          additional extra large loads from the XLPL tariff.          The recommendations ask the
    5          Commission to treat a definitional exclusion as a prohibition, and that proposition should
    6          not be adopted by implication.
    7
    8    Q.    How should the Commission address the argument that the tariff is broader than the
    9          statutory definition?
   10    A.    The Commission should evaluate both the statutory minimum and its existing ratemaking
   11          authority. HB 2992 establishes requirements for specified large-load customers and
   12          provides the minimum standards, but OG&E has proposed customer protections beyond
   13          the minimum standard to also address other loads that may create comparable service
   14          obligations and risks. The proposed classifications are intended to apply protections
   15          consistently where OG&E must plan for substantial incremental demand. If OG&E is
   16          going to add significant infrastructure to the grid to serve a customer, those significant
   17          investments create the need for the same customer protections we propose in the XLPL
   18          tariff and Terms and Conditions regardless of whether the XLPL customer is a
   19          cryptocurrency miner, a data center, manufacturer, or industrial. For example, if the Inola
   20          smelter were to be located in OG&E’s service territory, OG&E believes the protections of
   21          the XLPL Tariff and Terms and Conditions should apply to that project regardless of the
   22          definition of large load contained in HB 2992.
   23
   24    Q.    Does any responsive witness support basing applicability on load size rather than
   25          industry?
   26    A.    Yes. PAO witness Dismukes, who surveyed thirteen large load tariffs across the country,
   27          testifies that while some jurisdictions have limited their tariffs to data centers, most define
   28          applicability based on a minimum load size, irrespective of the industrial or economic

         Case No. PUD2026-000046

    1          sector of the end use. 3 He also finds that OG&E’s 75 MW threshold is equal to the median
    2          threshold approved nationwide. 4 His survey is consistent with OG&E’s approach: the
    3          protections apply because of the size of the service obligation, not the customer’s line of
    4          business.
    5
    6    Q.    Is Mr. Marchand’s concern about inadvertent capture of commercial facilities well
    7          founded?
    8    A.    No, and his objective is already satisfied.      Mr. Marchand explains that Walmart’s
    9          automated distribution facilities may approach or exceed 50 MW over a planning horizon,
   10          and he supports the 75 MW threshold because it buffers conventional commercial
   11          operations from this tariff. 5
   12                  OG&E agrees, and the tariff reflects it. No customer is subject to the XLPL tariff
   13          because of the kind of business it operates; a customer becomes subject to it only by
   14          satisfying the Customer Type 1, 2, or 3 criteria, each of which requires a service obligation
   15          of 75 MW or more. A facility at the demand levels Mr. Marchand describes is not captured.
   16          The protection Walmart seeks is the 75 MW threshold, which OG&E proposed and
   17          continues to support,
   18
   19    Q.    Why did OG&E include a Type 2 customer and why are the Type 2 customer
   20          parameters appropriate?
   21    A.    Customer Type 2 is necessary because an existing customer can create the same
   22          incremental service obligation and stranded-cost risk as a new customer. The tariff should
   23          not turn solely on whether the customer is new to OG&E’s system. If an existing customer
   24          adds at least 75 MW, or grows to a total demand level at which OG&E must plan for a
   25          materially different service obligation, OG&E must procure capacity, preserve
   26          transmission capability, and assume long-term planning risk in the same way it would for
   27          a new customer. The Type 2 parameters prevent a customer from avoiding XLPL

    1          protections merely because some portion of its load existed before July 1, 2026. That is
    2          particularly important because the risks addressed by the tariff are forward-looking: the
    3          incremental planning obligation, not the customer’s historical status, is what creates
    4          exposure for other customer classes.
    5
    6    Q.    Why does Customer Type 2 include an existing customer whose demand increases
    7          and whose total demand is 125 MW or more?
    8    A.    The 125 MW criterion prevents an existing customer from avoiding the tariff by adding
    9          load in increments just below 75 MW. Without it, a customer currently taking 60 MW
   10          could add 70 MW, reaching 130 MW without ever triggering the tariff, even though OG&E
   11          would have to plan and procure for each addition just as it would for a single 70 MW
   12          increase.   The criterion serves the same anti-avoidance purpose as the aggregation
   13          provision: the tariff should turn on the size of the obligation OG&E must serve, not on how
   14          the customer sequences its growth.
   15                  OIEC witness Dauphinais observes that a customer with total demand of 125 MW
   16          or more would become subject to the tariff if it increases its demand by any amount. 6 That
   17          is by design. A customer of that size already represents an XLPL-scale service obligation,
   18          and growth in that obligation is precisely what the tariff’s protections are intended to
   19          address. PAO witness Dismukes would limit qualification for existing customers to
   20          incremental load of 75 MW or more, 7 which would eliminate this criterion and reopen the
   21          avoidance path it closes.
   22
   23    Q.    How is the Customer Type 2 baseline determined?
   24    A.    The billing-demand baseline is the customer’s maximum metered demand during the 12
   25          months before July 1, 2026. That objective historical measure provides a practical
   26          reference point for determining whether an existing customer’s future demand meets the
   27          tariff threshold.



         6
               Dauphinais Responsive, 21:9–13.
         7
               Dismukes Responsive, 19:3–5.
         Rebuttal Testimony of Kimber L. Shoop                                               Page 7 of 34

    1    Q.    Does the use of incremental load to determine whether an existing customer qualifies
    2          as Customer Type 2 mean that only the incremental portion of the customer’s load is
    3          subject to the XLPL tariff?
    4    A.    No. As OG&E witness Gwin Cash explains, incremental load is relevant to whether an
    5          existing customer qualifies for the tariff; it does not establish a permanent boundary
    6          limiting the tariff to only that increment. Once the customer qualifies, OG&E serves and
    7          plans for the customer under a single ESA and a single Billing Contract Demand. The
    8          tariff’s minimum billing obligations, collateral requirements, and termination protections
    9          therefore apply to the customer’s full-service obligation, not merely the portion of load
   10          added after the baseline period.
   11
   12    Q.    Why is Customer Type 3 necessary?
   13    A.    Customer Type 3 addresses circumstances in which an existing customer’s service
   14          conditions cause OG&E to obtain at least 75 MW of additional capacity even without a
   15          conventional increase in metered load. Examples may include changes in load-reduction
   16          treatment, resource-adequacy requirements, or other service conditions. Without Type 3,
   17          materially similar capacity obligations could receive materially different treatment. For
   18          example, a current cryptocurrency miner may be able to take service under OG&E’s load
   19          reduction tariff. As this Commission is aware, the SPP rules around how OG&E can count
   20          load reduction customers toward its accredited capacity is changing and it is possible that
   21          those rules change so that either OG&E can no longer count that load reduction customer
   22          capacity as a load modifying resource, or the customer could decide to leave the load
   23          reduction program. Either way, it could mean that OG&E needs to add generating capacity
   24          for that existing customer. Similarly, it is possible that a cryptocurrency miner decides to
   25          stay at the same MW load level, but switch to data center operation with different usage
   26          patterns that prevent continued reliance on load reduction. This change in operation could
   27          also require OG&E to add new generating capacity. In such scenarios, the customer
   28          predates the creation of the XLPL Tariff and has not changed its overall demand. But
   29          either SPP’s evolving rules or the customer’s change in energy usage warrants inclusion in

    1          the XLPL Tariff as a Type 3 customer and the necessary protections that the XLPL Tariff
    2          provides.
    3
    4    Q.    PAO witness Dismukes recommends rejecting Customer Type 3 because none of the
    5          tariffs in his survey include a comparable category. How do you respond?
    6    A.    Mr. Dismukes is correct that OG&E is not aware of another commission that has approved
    7          a comparable qualification standard, and OG&E acknowledged as much in discovery. 8 But
    8          the absence of a comparable provision elsewhere reflects the circumstances OG&E faces
    9          rather than a flaw in the provision. As Mr. Dismukes recounts, two of the three scenarios
   10          OG&E identified involve SPP’s treatment of load reduction as a load modifier and SPP’s
   11          planning reserve margin requirements. 9 Those are features of OG&E’s position in SPP
   12          and of its existing Load Reduction program. A survey of tariffs developed in other regions,
   13          under other resource adequacy constructs, would not be expected to address them. The
   14          question for the Commission is not whether another jurisdiction has faced the same
   15          problem, but whether the problem exists here. OG&E believes it does, and that an existing
   16          customer whose change in service conditions requires OG&E to add 75 MW or more of
   17          capacity presents the same planning obligation as a new customer of that size. It should be
   18          noted that OG&E in particular has been successful in maximizing its load reduction
   19          program. That program’s success reduces the amount of capacity that OG&E must have
   20          to meet its reliability requirements. If the rules change and we can no longer count on that
   21          same level of load modifying customer load reduction, OG&E should be able to reclassify
   22          those customers as Type 3 to ensure the XLPL customer protections are in place for any
   23          increased capacity needs driven by that large load customer.
   24
   25    Q.    What is OG&E’s position on notice for a Type 3 determination?
   26    A.    OG&E would support a single, consolidated, administratively workable notice to the
   27          customer and the Director of PUD that identifies the service-condition change, the capacity
   28          OG&E determines must be added, and the basis for the Type 3 classification, while

    1          preserving the Commission’s existing authority to resolve disputes. Any process should
    2          avoid delaying resource planning or creating uncertainty about the customer’s service
    3          obligations.
    4
    5    Q.    Some parties object to OG&E’s ability to aggregate loads in certain circumstances.
    6          Why did OG&E recommend that the Commission approve that aggregation
    7          capability?
    8    A.    OG&E wanted to avoid a potential customer’s ability to evade the XLPL Tariff by splitting
    9          up loads between different locations. If a 200 MW data center decides to split the load at
   10          three different sites, OG&E must add all the same infrastructure (and perhaps more) to
   11          serve the load regardless of its divided location. In such cases, it is necessary to have an
   12          option to aggregate those loads to ensure that the same customer protections apply. OG&E
   13          believes this aggregation capability is important to avoid gamification or strategies that
   14          intentionally try to evade the XLPL tariff. OG&E has not designed this aggregation
   15          capability with the ability to aggregate loads that by their very nature are and should be
   16          located in different locations, e.g., Walmart stores. OG&E would be happy to ensure that
   17          this aggregation capability is properly limited or subject to Commission review so that
   18          customers have the ability to protest any aggregation at the appropriate time.
   19
   20    Q.    What is your recommendation to the Commission regarding applicability?
   21    A.    OG&E recommends that the Commission approve the tariff’s applicability provisions as
   22          filed, including all three customer types, the Customer Type 2 criterion for an existing
   23          customer whose demand increases and whose total demand is 125 MW or more, the
   24          Customer Type 3 provisions with a single consolidated notice process, and the aggregation
   25          provision. The Commission should decline to adopt definitional exclusions or other
   26          limitations that would leave comparable extra-large service obligations without
   27          comparable customer protections.

    1             RESOURCE ADEQUACY, ESA REVIEW, AND LOAD RAMP DELAY
    2    Q.    Please summarize the recommendations you address in this section.
    3    A.    OIEC witness James Dauphinais makes three related recommendations.                      First, he
    4          recommends that OG&E be required to provide, with each executed ESA, an analysis
    5          demonstrating it has sufficient existing and planned resources to serve the new XLPL
    6          customer’s load at its contracted ramp level and its fully ramped load through the end of
    7          the initial term. 10 Second, he recommends that OG&E provide a complete copy of each
    8          executed ESA to PUD Staff at least one year prior to commencement of service, with a 30-
    9          day review period for all parties to this Case and a 15-day window in which to move for
   10          Commission review. 11 Third, he recommends that the T&CXLLC and XLPL tariff be
   11          amended to give OG&E a unilateral right to delay a customer’s load ramp to maintain
   12          resource adequacy if the in-service date of necessary production resource additions is
   13          delayed. 12
   14
   15    Q.    First, Mr. Dauphinais states that neither the tariff nor the T&CXLLC requires
   16          OG&E to demonstrate it can serve a new XLPL load while maintaining resource
   17          adequacy. Is that accurate?
   18    A.    It is accurate as a description of the tariff language, but it does not follow that the obligation
   19          is absent. OG&E’s obligation to maintain resource adequacy arises from SPP’s Resource
   20          Adequacy requirements and from the Company’s obligation to serve, and it applies to
   21          OG&E’s system as a whole regardless of what any individual tariff says. The XLPL tariff
   22          does not diminish it.
   23                  The forum in which that obligation is examined is also well established. OG&E’s
   24          resource planning is reviewed through the Integrated Resource Planning process under
   25          OAC 165:35-37, under which the Company files an IRP every three years and files interim
   26          updates when material changes in planning assumptions occur.               OG&E’s 2026 IRP,
   27          submitted as an update, forecasts a need for incremental generation capacity driven in part

    7    Q.    Mr. Dauphinais notes that Section 4.01(a) of the standard form ESA contemplates
    8          procurement of interim capacity. 13 Does that provision suggest OG&E could commit
    9          to serve a load it cannot reliably serve?
   10    A.    No. That provision addresses the timing mismatch that can arise between when a
   11          customer’s load begins and when longer-lead resources reach commercial operation, and it
   12          provides that interim capacity may be procured outside competitive bidding requirements
   13          to facilitate the timing of the customer’s need. It is a tool for meeting the obligation, not a
   14          substitute for it. OG&E confirmed in discovery that in the event of a delay in completion
   15          or interconnection of a new generation resource, it would seek procurement of interim
   16          capacity resources.
   17                  I would add that the provision is expressly subject to the cost protections elsewhere
   18          in the Agreement. Section 4.01(a) provides that interim capacity shall be included in the
   19          Fuel Adjustment Clause and that any impact on other customer classes will be mitigated as
   20          described in the Agreement — that is, through the same Commission review of adverse
   21          rate impacts that Section 506 establishes.

    1    Q.    Please address Mr. Dauphinais’ second recommendation that OG&E provide a
    2          complete copy of each executed ESA to PUD Staff at least one year prior to
    3          commencement of service, with a 30-day review period for all parties to this Case and
    4          a 15-day window in which to move for Commission review. Do you have any
    5          concerns?
    6    A.    Yes. The ESAs contain highly sensitive, customer-specific commercial information. Each
    7          agreement sets out the customer’s Maximum Contract Demand, its Contract Demand
    8          Schedule showing load ramp by period, the identity and location of the site, the form and
    9          amount of collateral posted, and the identity of any parental guarantor and its credit
   10          standing. Taken together, that is a detailed picture of a customer’s planned buildout, its
   11          financing posture, and its operational timeline.
   12                  The sensitivity of this category of information is well established on this record.
   13          When OIEC sought comparable information in discovery, OG&E produced it as Highly
   14          Sensitive Confidential and, to protect customer identities and commercially sensitive future
   15          plans, made it available only through a secure portal that prohibited downloading, copying,
   16          photographing, screen capture, recording, transcription, or reproduction outside the portal.
   17          Mr. Dauphinais himself observed that limitation and declined to reproduce the attachment
   18          in his exhibits.
   19                  Mr. Dauphinais’s proposal would distribute the underlying agreements
   20          considerably more broadly. He recommends circulating each executed ESA to all parties
   21          to this Case, subject to the protective order. OIEC is described in his own testimony as an
   22          unincorporated association consisting of a diverse group of large consumers of energy, and
   23          Walmart, and Google are parties of this case. These are parties whose members and
   24          affiliates may include commercial counterparties, competitors for sites, or competitors for
   25          the same constrained supply of generation equipment and interconnection capacity as the
   26          XLPL customer whose agreement is being reviewed.
   27
   28    Q.    Would a protective order adequately address that concern?
   29    A.    No. A protective order manages the risk; it does not eliminate it, and OG&E does not
   30          believe the Commission should have to rely on it where the benefit on the other side of the

    1          ledger is as limited as it is here. The relevant question is what the disclosure accomplishes.
    2          If the ESA is executed on a Commission-approved form, and the material terms are fixed
    3          by that form, then the incremental information the review would surface is precisely the
    4          customer-specific commercial detail that is most sensitive and least necessary to the

     Stories about electricity prices continue to dominate headlines, and rightly so — consumers across the country are

     restructured toward electric sector deregulation and sometimes retail competition, where customers were allowed to

     For years, proponents of deregulation have promised that competition would drive down prices for consumers. The

        What Does “Deregulation” Mean?
        The practice of deregulating the electric sector occurred on a state-by-state level, largely in the early 2000s.
        In practical terms, deregulation meant that electric utilities were forced to divest their power plants and were
        thereafter prohibited from owning any form of electric generation.

        The theory behind electric sector deregulation was that a “competitive” wholesale generation market would
        drive prices down for consumers.

        In practice, though, competition has not resulted in the outcome of lower prices that its architects promised.
        Instead, residential customers in deregulated states are paying significantly more than customers in states
        that have kept the traditional, regulated utility model — and the gap is growing.

        In this paper, deregulation is discussed as both a market construct and a state-level political decision.
        References to “deregulated states” and “deregulated markets” are used interchangeably.

   The Big Picture: Who is Feeling
   the Impact of Price Increases?
   The impact of deregulation on residential customers is stark when viewed at the national level of average prices.
   In 2025, across all 50 states plus the District of Columbia (DC), the average residential price in deregulated states
   was 23.41 cents per kilowatt-hour, compared to just 14.60 cents in regulated states — a gap of nearly 9 cents per
   kilowatt-hour.

   The national average residential electricity price in 2025 was 17.92 cents/kWh — a figure shaped by two opposing
   forces: deregulated states, which pushed the average up, and regulated states, which held it down.

   Interestingly, the full nationwide comparison actually understates the case against deregulation: the regulated-
   state average includes outliers like Hawaii and Alaska, whose locations have naturally resulted in higher prices
   — driven by geography and fuel logistics, not market structure. These outliers work to pull the regulated average
   up and narrow the apparent gap; strip them out, and the story only gets more dire for residential customers in
   deregulated states in the contiguous U.S.


   Why does a residential price gap exist
   between deregulated and regulated states?

   The answer lies in how the different electric model structures handle accountability, planning, and cost recovery.
   In regulated states, vertically integrated utilities plan generation, transmission, and distribution together under
   cost-of-service regulation. A state public utility commission reviews utility costs for prudency and authorizes rates
   to recover only what is reasonable and necessary to serve customers reliably. In this structure, utilities have an
   obligation to serve all customers and must conduct integrated planning decades into the future. This model is the
   original public-private partnership and ensures that utilities provide a reliable critical service at only reasonable
   and approved costs to customers.

   Deregulated markets work differently. Electric generation is bought and sold via wholesale markets, and
   residential customers are either simply takers of that market supply or, in some states, they can select their electric
   supplier – a structure referred to as retail choice.

   When the market is the supplier of electricity, customers are exposed to two fundamental issues that the regulated
   structure guards against: market volatility and scarcity pricing. In markets, prices result from balancing supply
   and demand — a mechanism that works well enough for ordinary consumer goods. But electricity isn’t an
   ordinary good. It’s an essential good, and essential goods tend to have “inelastic” demand: customers can’t
   simply substitute something else when prices rise because no substitute exists. That inelasticity is precisely what
   allows electricity prices to spike so sharply under certain conditions — as is happening now, with electric markets
   struggling to bring on adequate supply rather than curb demand, driving prices upward.

   State utility regulation exists specifically to interrupt this dynamic. Commissions of regulators exist to review utility
   costs and authorize customer rates under an explicit mandate to keep them just and reasonable. Deregulated
   states forgo that buffer on the supply side. Instead, electricity is priced by the market itself, and when supply
   tightens or volatility hits, there’s no regulator positioned to reduce the impact of electric supply price shocks.

     Methodology
     Power for Tomorrow’s analysis draws entirely on publicly available data from the U.S. Energy Information
     Administration’s (EIA) Electric Power Monthly, specifically the February 2026 release. In this monthly release, Power
     for Tomorrow collected full calendar-year 2025 data through the December year-to-date average, and compared
     it against the same period in 2024.

     EIA’s residential price figures are themselves built from surveys of utilities across the country, capturing the
     average rate charged by all utilities offering residential electric service within a given state — making this one of
     the most comprehensive and consistently reported data sets available on actual electricity costs paid by American
     households.

     For purposes of this analysis, “deregulated” refers to states with a restructured, RTO/ISO-based competitive
     generation market, while all other states are treated as traditionally regulated, vertically integrated utility markets.
     Where a contiguous U.S. (lower 48 + DC) view is presented, Alaska and Hawaii are excluded — not to manipulate
     the comparison, but because their extreme prices reflect unique geographic and fuel-logistics realities rather than
     the effects of market structure and including them would otherwise distort national comparisons in ways unrelated
     to the deregulation question this analysis is examining.




     Conclusion
     Using state-level, average residential electric price data available for both 2025 and 2024, there is clear evidence
     about the impact of deregulation on residential electric customers. The problem is structural, not temporary: In
     the contiguous U.S., residential customers in deregulated states paid 60.4% more on average for electricity than
     residential customers im regulated states — a gap of nearly 9 cents per kilowatt.

     Further, nine of the ten most expensive states in the contiguous U.S. are deregulated, while all of the ten cheapest
     are regulated. And the trend is not correcting itself — it is accelerating, with deregulated prices climbing at nearly
     twice the rate of regulated states from 2024 to 2025, even before the full effects of data center and large load
     growth have worked their way into the numbers. As demand pressure builds in the years ahead, deregulated
     markets — already worse at controlling costs today — are the ones least equipped to absorb it without passing the
     burden directly to residential customers.

     The evidence is no longer ambiguous: deregulation has not delivered on its central promise. It has not lowered
     prices for the people it was meant to help. It has raised them, and it is poised to keep raising them faster than the
     regulated alternative it was supposed to outperform.
